Title: Ishtar Gate
Description: The glazed-brick gate of Nebuchadnezzar II's Babylon was excavated by a German team under Robert Koldewey. Its fragments were packed into barrels and shipped to Berlin, where the front gate was rebuilt inside the museum. Iraq has repeatedly asked Germany to return it, notably in 2002 and 2009.

Title: Pergamon Altar
Description: Carl Humann excavated the altar between 1878 and 1886. Under an agreement between the Ottoman Empire and the German government, its relief panels were shipped to Berlin, where they became the centrepiece of the museum named after them. Turkish culture ministers demanded its return in 1998 and 2001.

Title: Market Gate of Miletus
Description: This Roman marble gateway once led into the southern market of Miletus. It was excavated by German archaeologists in 1903, and its fragments were transported to Berlin in 1907–1908 and reassembled as a full-size monument inside the museum.

Title: Mshatta Facade
Description: The carved stone facade of an Umayyad desert palace was given by the Ottoman Sultan Abdülhamid II to Emperor Wilhelm II, a gift that reflected the two empires' political alliance rather than the wishes of the people living in the region. A large part of it was brought to Berlin in 1903.

Title: Bust of Nefertiti
Description: Found in 1912 in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose by a German team led by Ludwig Borchardt, the bust came to Berlin through a division of finds with the French-led Egyptian Antiquities Service. Egypt has demanded its return since 1924, accusing Borchardt of concealing its value; Berlin insists on its ownership.

Title: Benin Bronzes
Description: Thousands of plaques and sculptures were looted from the royal palace by British forces in 1897 and sold on to museums across Europe; Berlin acquired one of the largest collections. In 2022 Germany transferred ownership of the Benin Bronzes in its public collections to Nigeria. Some have been physically returned, while others remain in Berlin on loan.

Title: Ngonnso statue
Description: The statue of Ngonnso, the founding queen mother of the Nso people, was taken in 1902 during a military expedition of the German colonial army and donated to the Berlin museum. After decades of campaigning by the Nso community, the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation authorised its return in 2022; the physical handover was still pending in late 2024.
Credit: Historical photo: Felix von Luschan, public domain

Title: Luf boat
Description: This large ocean-going outrigger boat was built on Luf, a community that had been devastated by a German naval punitive expedition in 1882–1883. It was brought to Berlin in 1904. Historian Götz Aly's book Das Prachtboot (2021) sparked a public debate about whether its acquisition can be called legitimate.

Title: Giraffatitan skeleton
Description: The world's tallest mounted dinosaur skeleton was dug up in German East Africa by a colonial expedition that relied on hundreds of local labourers. German and Tanzanian commentators have questioned the museum's claim to rightful ownership, although Tanzania has not submitted an official return request.

Title: Sphinx of Hattusa
Description: Two sphinxes from the southern gate of the Hittite capital were taken to Germany for restoration in 1917. One was sent back in 1924, but the other stayed in Berlin and was displayed in the Pergamonmuseum from 1934. After years of pressure from Turkey, it was returned in 2011 and reunited with its pair near its original site.
